title: Streams, pipelines, expansions, and your first scripts
goal: Redirect and pipe command output, predict every shell expansion, and create, run and debug your first Bash script that uses its command line arguments.

topics.title: Streams, redirection, pipelines and tees
topics.examNote: Quiz 1 Q2D: *overwrite myfile with OOPS using a redirection* (`echo OOPS > myfile`). Quiz 1 Q3B (2 marks): a single pipeline with `cut`, `sort`, `tee` and `head` built from an English description. Expect fd numbers, `2>&1` order and `/dev/null` as short answers. Assignment 3 requires error messages on **standard error** (`>&2`, introduced here); you will write those messages in scripts on Day 5.

blocks.text:
### Everything is a stream of bytes

A **byte stream** is an ordered sequence of bytes (characters). Programs read data from streams and write data to streams. Every command you run starts with **three standard streams** already connected for it:

| Stream | Short name | File descriptor | Connected by default to |
|---|---|---|---|
| standard input | stdin | `0` | the keyboard |
| standard output | stdout | `1` | the terminal |
| standard error | stderr | `2` | the terminal |

A **file descriptor** is just a small integer that names an open stream. Memorize the three numbers: **0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr**. You will use them in redirections.

Normal results go to **stdout**. Error and diagnostic messages go to **stderr**. Because both stdout and stderr are connected to the terminal by default, they *look* the same on screen, but they are two separate streams that you can send to different places.

blocks.code:
$ ls classlist zzz
ls: cannot access 'zzz': No such file or directory
classlist
blocks.caption: The error line was written to stderr (fd 2); the line classlist was written to stdout (fd 1). Both appear on the terminal.

blocks.text: Some commands read **standard input** when you do not give them a file name. If you type `sort` and press Enter, `sort` waits for you to type lines on the keyboard. You signal the end of input by pressing **Ctrl + D** at the start of a line; then `sort` prints the lines in sorted order. (Ctrl + C would instead stop `sort` without printing anything.)
Type `sort` and press Enter. Type `zebra`, `elephant`, `anteater` and `dog`, pressing Enter after each. Then press **Ctrl + D**. The four words come back in alphabetical order.

blocks.q: What are the file descriptor numbers of stdin, stdout and stderr?
blocks.a: stdin is 0, stdout is 1, stderr is 2.

blocks.text:
### Redirecting standard output: `>` and `>>`

**Redirection** changes where a command reads its input from or sends its output to. To send standard output to a file, write `1> filename` (or just `> filename`; the `1` is optional) anywhere in the command:

- `>` **creates** the file if it does not exist, and **overwrites** (truncates) it if it does.
- `>>` **appends** to the end of the file instead of overwriting it (it also creates the file if needed).

The command itself does not know about the file. The shell opens the file and connects it to fd 1 *before* the command runs. Anything the command would have printed on stdout goes into the file instead, so nothing appears on the terminal.

blocks.code:
$ echo OOPS > myfile
$ cat myfile
OOPS
$ echo again >> myfile
$ cat myfile
OOPS
again
$ echo new > myfile
$ cat myfile
new
blocks.caption: Quiz 1 asked: what command overwrites myfile with the string OOPS? Answer: echo OOPS > myfile

blocks.text: In your practice folder, run `echo OOPS > myfile`, then `cat myfile`. Run `echo again >> myfile` and `cat myfile` again: two lines. Now run `echo new > myfile` and `cat myfile`: only `new` is left.

blocks.code:
$ ls -A 1> files.txt
$ ls -A > files.txt
blocks.caption: These two commands do the same thing: for stdout the 1 is optional.

blocks.q: What is the difference between `echo hi > f` and `echo hi >> f` when `f` already contains one line?
blocks.a: `>` overwrites: afterwards `f` contains only `hi`. `>>` appends: afterwards `f` contains its old line followed by `hi`.

blocks.text: `sort data > data` does **not** sort the file in place. The shell truncates `data` to empty *before* `sort` starts, so `sort` reads an empty file and `data` ends up empty. Write to a different file instead: `sort data > sorted`.

### Redirecting standard error: `2>`

To redirect standard error you **must** write the file descriptor `2`: `2> filename`. Then only the error messages go to the file; normal output still goes to the terminal.

You can redirect both streams of one command to **separate** files:

blocks.code:
$ ls -A zzz file?? > files.txt 2> error.txt
$ cat files.txt
file00
file01
$ cat error.txt
ls: cannot access 'zzz': No such file or directory
blocks.caption: Directory contains file00 and file01. Many commands keep going after an error, so ls still lists the files it can.

blocks.text:
**`/dev/null`** is the *null device*: a special file that discards everything written to it (and reports that the write succeeded). Use it to throw output away, most often error messages:

```bash
ls classlist zzz 2> /dev/null      # error message discarded, classlist still printed
```

blocks.q: Write a command that runs `ls zzz` and stores the error message in a file named `err.txt`.
blocks.a: `ls zzz 2> err.txt`

blocks.text:
### Both streams to one file: `> file 2>&1`

To send **all** output (stdout and stderr) to the same file, redirect stdout to the file and then add `2>&1`:

```bash
ls -A zzz file?? > all.txt 2>&1
```

`2>&1` means: *make file descriptor 2 a duplicate (copy) of file descriptor 1*, that is, send stderr to wherever stdout points **right now**.

The shell processes redirections **from left to right**, so order matters:

1. `> all.txt 2>&1`: first fd 1 points to `all.txt`; then fd 2 is copied from fd 1, so it also points to `all.txt`. Everything goes to the file.
2. `2>&1 > all.txt`: first fd 2 is copied from fd 1, which is still the **terminal**; then fd 1 is changed to `all.txt`. Errors still appear on the terminal and only normal output goes to the file.

Bash also has the shorthand `&> file`, which means the same as `> file 2>&1`. The course notebooks use the `> file 2>&1` form, so make sure you can write that one.

blocks.code:
$ ls -A zzz file?? 2>&1 > all.txt
ls: cannot access 'zzz': No such file or directory
$ cat all.txt
file00
file01
blocks.caption: Wrong order: the error still reaches the terminal.

blocks.q: Why does `2>&1 > all.txt` not send errors into all.txt?
blocks.a: Redirections are done left to right. When `2>&1` runs, fd 1 still points at the terminal, so fd 2 becomes a copy of *the terminal*. Changing fd 1 afterwards does not change fd 2; the copy was already made.

blocks.q: Write a command that sends both the output and the errors of `ls a b` into `log.txt`.
blocks.a: `ls a b > log.txt 2>&1` (or `ls a b &> log.txt`).

blocks.text:
### The other direction: `>&2`

`2>&1` sends standard error to wherever standard output goes. The reverse, `1>&2`, is usually written **`>&2`** (the `1` is optional, as always for stdout). It makes standard output a copy of standard error, so whatever the command prints goes to **stderr** instead of stdout:

```bash
echo "Something went wrong" >&2
```

On the screen this looks exactly like a normal `echo`. The difference shows when stdout is redirected or piped: the message still reaches the terminal, because it was never on stdout. Scripts use this to print their **error messages** (you will write such messages in scripts on Day 5).

blocks.code:
$ echo hello >&2 > out.txt
$ cat out.txt
hello
blocks.caption: Left to right again: >&2 sends stdout to the terminal's stderr, then > out.txt changes stdout to the file. The later redirection wins, so hello goes into out.txt.

blocks.text:
### Redirecting standard input: `<`

`0< filename` (or just `< filename`) makes the command read **standard input from the file** instead of the keyboard.

The examples from here on use a file named `classlist`: four students, one per line (it is shown in full a little further down). They also use **`wc -l`**: `wc` means *word count*, and with `-l` it counts **lines**. `wc -l FILE` prints the number of lines followed by the file name.

Most filter commands also accept a file name argument, so `sort unsorted.txt` and `sort < unsorted.txt` print the same thing. The difference shows up with commands that print the file name: `wc -l classlist` prints `4 classlist`, but `wc -l < classlist` prints just `4`, because `wc` reads stdin and never sees a file name.

You can combine input and output redirection: `sort < unsorted.txt > sorted.txt`.

blocks.code:
$ sort < unsorted.txt > sorted.txt
$ cat sorted.txt
anteater
dog
elephant
zebra
$ wc -l classlist
4 classlist
$ wc -l < classlist
4
blocks.caption: unsorted.txt contains zebra, elephant, anteater, dog (one per line); classlist has 4 lines.

blocks.q: Why does `wc -l < classlist` print only a number while `wc -l classlist` also prints the name?
blocks.a: With `<` the shell opens the file and connects it to stdin; `wc` only sees an anonymous stream, so it has no file name to print.

blocks.text:
### Pipelines: `|`

A **pipe** `|` connects the **standard output** of the command on its left to the **standard input** of the command on its right. A **pipeline** is a chain of commands joined by pipes. Think of each command as a segment of pipe: data flows in one end, gets changed, and flows out the other end.

```bash
ls /bin /usr/bin | sort | uniq | wc -l
```

Only **stdout** goes through a pipe. Error messages on stderr still go to the terminal (unless you redirect them).

The commands that sit in the middle of pipelines are called **filters**: they read stdin (or files named as arguments), transform the lines, and write stdout. These are the ones you need:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sort` | sorts lines (alphabetically by default) |
| `sort -n` | sorts numerically (so `9` comes before `10`) |
| `sort -r` | reverse order; `sort -n -r` (or `-nr`) is largest number first |
| `uniq` | removes **adjacent** duplicate lines (so `sort` first!) |
| `uniq -d` | prints only lines that are duplicated (one copy each) |
| `wc -l` | counts lines |
| `head -n 3` | first 3 lines (`head -n3` also works) |
| `tail -n 3` | last 3 lines |
| `cut -f 3` | 3rd field of each line; fields are separated by **TAB** by default |
| `cut -d" " -f 1` | 1st field, using a space as the delimiter (`-d` = `--delimiter`, `-f` = `--fields`) |

`cut -f1,3` selects several fields, and `cut -f2 -d:` uses `:` as the delimiter (options can come in either order).

blocks.code:
$ cat classlist
Cade	Barry	3100025
Day	Holly	2999999
Friese	Andy	3001111
Yu	Sue	1990000
$ cut -f3 classlist
3100025
2999999
3001111
1990000
$ cut -f3 classlist | sort
1990000
2999999
3001111
3100025
$ cut -f3 classlist | sort -r | head -n1
3100025
blocks.caption: classlist fields are separated by single TAB characters.

blocks.q: Why must you usually `sort` before `uniq`?
blocks.a: `uniq` only removes duplicates that are **next to each other**. Sorting puts identical lines together so `uniq` can find them all.

blocks.text:
The next examples need a few lines of numbers. **`printf`** is a printing command like `echo`, but it does not add a newline by itself: you write `
` wherever you want a line break. So `printf '10
9
100
'` prints the three lines `10`, `9` and `100`. It is a handy way to feed test lines into a pipeline.

blocks.code:
$ printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort
10
100
9
$ printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort -n
9
10
100
blocks.caption: Plain sort compares character by character (1 < 9), so 100 comes before 9. Use -n for numbers.

blocks.text: `sort` without `-n` sorts numbers as text: `100` comes before `9`. Student numbers that all have the same number of digits sort correctly either way, but marks like 9, 72, 100 need `sort -n`.

### Tees: save *and* pass along

Redirection sends output to a file; a pipe sends it to another command. To do **both**, use `tee`. The `tee` command reads standard input and copies it to **standard output and to one or more files**. Like the letter T in plumbing, the data continues down the pipeline while a copy is saved.

Because `tee` is an ordinary command, you can put it anywhere in a pipeline to save an intermediate result:

```bash
date | tee fulldate.txt | cut -d" " -f1
fortune | tee fortune.txt | cowsay | tee cow.txt | cowsay -n
```

### Building a pipeline from an English description

Quiz 1 asked: *extract the student numbers from `classlist`, sort them ascending, save all of them to a file `snum` (in sorted order), and print the first three.* Translate each phrase into one command, in order:

1. extract the student numbers: `cut -f3 classlist`
2. sort ascending: `sort`
3. save all of them (sorted) and keep going: `tee snum`
4. print only the first three: `head -n3`

blocks.caption: The tee must come AFTER sort (the file must be sorted) and BEFORE head (the file must contain all the numbers).

blocks.text:
Make the class list yourself: `printf 'Cade	Barry	3100025
Day	Holly	2999999
Friese	Andy	3001111
Yu	Sue	1990000
' > classlist` (`	` is a TAB). Then run `cut -f3 classlist | sort | tee snum | head -n3` and `cat snum`.

blocks.q: Why would `cut -f3 classlist | sort | head -n3 | tee snum` lose marks?
blocks.a: `tee` would only see the three lines that `head` let through, so `snum` would contain three numbers instead of all of them.

blocks.q: Write a pipeline that prints how many lines in `words.txt` are different (count of distinct lines).
blocks.a: `sort words.txt | uniq | wc -l`

blocks.text:
### Key points

- fd **0** = stdin, **1** = stdout, **2** = stderr.
- `>` overwrites, `>>` appends, `<` reads stdin from a file, `2>` redirects errors, `2> /dev/null` discards them.
- `> file 2>&1` puts both streams in one file; redirections are processed **left to right**. `>&2` sends stdout to stderr.
- `|` connects stdout to the next command's stdin; stderr does not go through the pipe.
- `tee file` saves a copy of the stream and passes it on; place it exactly where the data has the form you want saved.

topics.title: Shell expansions
topics.examNote: Know the **order** of the seven expansions and which happen inside double quotes. Quiz 1 used command substitution (`perm=$(stat -c %a "$src")`, Q4) and arithmetic expansion (`$(( ... / 2 ))`, Q3A) inside scripts; you will write those once variables (Day 4) are covered. "What does this print?" questions on brace expansion and word splitting are easy marks.

blocks.text:
### What is an expansion?

The shell splits each command line into **tokens** (words and operators). Before running the command, it performs **expansions**: it replaces some tokens with new strings. For example, in `echo $((1 + 1))`, the shell replaces `$((1 + 1))` with `2` and then runs `echo 2`. The command never sees the original text.

There are **seven** kinds of expansion, performed **in this order** (memorize it):

1. **brace expansion**: `{a,b}`, `{1..5}`
2. **tilde expansion**: `~`
3. **parameter expansion**: `$name`, `${name}`
4. **command substitution**: `$(command)`
5. **arithmetic expansion**: `$(( expression ))`
6. **word splitting**
7. **filename expansion** (globbing): `*`, `?`, `[...]`

Command substitution and arithmetic expansion have the **same precedence**: if a line has several of them, they are done left to right.

A memory aid: **B**rave **T**urtles **P**addle **C**alm **A**rctic **W**ater **F**ast (Brace, Tilde, Parameter, Command, Arithmetic, Word splitting, Filename).

blocks.q: List the seven expansions in order.
blocks.a: Brace, tilde, parameter, command substitution, arithmetic (same level as command substitution), word splitting, filename expansion.

blocks.text: Run `echo {a,b,c}`, `echo {9..0}` and `echo file{1..3}.txt`. Then, in your practice folder, run `mkdir week{01..03}` and `ls`.

### Brace expansion

Brace expansion **generates strings that follow a pattern**. Its form is *preamble*`{`*expression*`}`*postscript*. The optional preamble is glued to the front of every generated string and the optional postscript to the back. The *expression* is either:

- two or more **comma-separated** strings: `{a,b,c}`, or
- a **sequence expression** `{x..y}` or `{x..y..incr}` where `x` and `y` are integers or single characters and `incr` is an optional step size.

Brace expansion is pure text generation. Unlike `*`, it does **not** look at which files exist.

blocks.caption: The last one is a nested brace expansion from the Bash manual.

blocks.text:
Leading zeros are kept: `{01..12}` gives `01 02 ... 12`. Two brace expansions next to each other give every combination, which is handy for creating many files or directories at once:

```bash
mkdir {2019..2022}-{01..12}     # 48 directories 2019-01 ... 2022-12
touch file{00..30}.txt          # file00.txt ... file30.txt
```

blocks.code:
$ echo {a,b}{1,2}
a1 a2 b1 b2

blocks.q: What does `echo x{1..3}y` print?
blocks.a: `x1y x2y x3y`

blocks.text:
### Tilde expansion

A `~` at the start of a word expands to the absolute path of **your home directory** (the value of `HOME`). `~username` expands to the home directory of *username*.

```bash
$ echo ~            # if your home directory is /home/user1
/home/user1
$ echo ~/notes
/home/user1/notes
```

### Parameter expansion

**Parameter expansion** happens when you get the value of a variable or parameter by writing `$name` (or `${name}`). You have already used one: `$?`, the exit status (Day 1).

A **variable** is a name that holds a string. Just enough to follow today's examples:

- `name=value` stores *value* in the variable *name*. There must be **no spaces around `=`**.
- `$name` is replaced by the stored value. A name that was never given a value expands to nothing.

Day 4 covers variables properly. Later today, `$1`, `$2`, ... in a script (the command line arguments) are parameter expansions too.

blocks.code:
$ course=CISC220
$ echo "I am taking $course"
I am taking CISC220

blocks.q: What does `x=5; echo x $x` print?
blocks.a: `x 5`. The first `x` is just a word; `$x` is replaced by the value `5`.

blocks.text: Brace expansion happens **first**, before variables are expanded. So `n=3; echo {1..$n}` prints `{1..3}` literally: when brace expansion ran, the text was `{1..$n}`, which is not a valid sequence, so it was left alone.

### Command substitution: `$( )`

`$(command)` runs *command* (in a subshell) and **replaces itself with the command's standard output**. Trailing newlines are removed. This is how you use a command's output inside a string, or store it in a variable:

```bash
echo "Today is $(date +%A), it's $(date +%H:%M)"   # date +%A prints the weekday, +%H:%M the time
moo=$(cowsay "Mooooo!")     # prints nothing: the output is stored in moo
echo "$moo"                 # now print it
```

blocks.code:
$ echo "classlist has $(wc -l < classlist) lines"
classlist has 4 lines
$ n=$(cut -f3 classlist | sort | head -n1)
$ echo "smallest student number: $n"
smallest student number: 1990000
blocks.caption: Using the 4-line classlist from the Streams lesson.

blocks.q: What is the difference between `x=$(date)` and `x=date`?
blocks.a: `x=$(date)` runs `date` and stores its output; `x=date` stores the four-letter string `date`.

blocks.text:
### Arithmetic expansion: `$(( ))`

`$(( expression ))` evaluates an **integer** arithmetic expression and substitutes the result. Division throws away the remainder (`7 / 2` is `3`); `%` gives the remainder. Arithmetic is rare at the command line but common in scripts (Day 5 covers arithmetic in full).

```bash
$ echo $(( 1 + 1 ))
2
$ mkdir dir$((2 * 5))       # creates dir10
```

blocks.q: What does `echo $(( 17 / 5 )) $(( 17 % 5 ))` print?
blocks.a: `3 2` (integer division, then remainder).

blocks.text:
### Word splitting

After the earlier expansions, **anything not inside double quotes** undergoes **word splitting**: the result is split into separate words (fields) wherever there are field separator characters. By default the separators are **space, tab and newline**, stored in the variable `IFS` (*internal field separator*). Several separators in a row count as **one** separator.

This is why spaces in file names cause trouble. `unzip CISC220 Assignment solutions.zip` gives `unzip` three arguments (`CISC220`, `Assignment`, `solutions.zip`). Quoting or escaping prevents the split.

blocks.code:
$ str="field1    field2       field3


field4"
$ echo $str
field1 field2 field3 field4
$ echo "$str"
field1    field2       field3


field4
blocks.caption: Unquoted: the runs of spaces and newlines became single word breaks, and echo joins its arguments with one space. Quoted: one argument, printed exactly.

blocks.text:
You can change `IFS` temporarily to split on something else, such as commas. Save the old value in another variable and put it back afterwards:

```bash
str="123456,Ester,Polly"
OLDIFS=$IFS      # save the normal separators
IFS=","         # split on commas only
echo $str        # prints: 123456 Ester Polly
IFS=$OLDIFS      # restore normal word splitting
```

Unquoted, `$str` is split at the commas into three words, and `echo` prints them separated by spaces. (The notebook also feeds the three words to a `for` loop; loops are Day 6.)

blocks.q: Why does `echo $(cut -f3 classlist)` print all the student numbers on one line?
blocks.a: The command substitution is unquoted, so its output is word split on the newlines. `echo` receives four separate arguments and prints them separated by single spaces.

blocks.text:
### Filename expansion

The **last** expansion is filename expansion: words containing `*`, `?` or `[...]` are replaced with the matching file names (Day 2). Because it comes after word splitting, a variable that holds `*` expands to file names when used unquoted.

### What happens inside quotes?

| | brace | tilde | parameter `$x` | command `$( )` | arithmetic `$(( ))` | word splitting | filename `*` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| unquoted | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `"double"` | no | no | **yes** | **yes** | **yes** | no | no |
| `'single'` | no | no | no | no | no | no | no |

Double quotes keep `$` working (parameter, command and arithmetic expansion) but **prevent word splitting and filename expansion** (and brace and tilde expansion). That is exactly why the course writes `"$var"`: the value is used as **one** word, exactly as stored, even if it contains spaces or `*`.

blocks.code:
$ echo "{a,b}" "~" '$HOME' "$((2+3))"
{a,b} ~ $HOME 5
$ v='f*'
$ echo "$v"
f*
$ echo $v
f1 f2
blocks.caption: The directory contains files f1 and f2.

blocks.q: Which expansions still happen inside double quotes?
blocks.a: Parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion (the ones that start with `$`).

blocks.text:
### Key points

- Order: **brace, tilde, parameter, command substitution / arithmetic, word splitting, filename**.
- Brace expansion generates text (`{a,b}`, `{1..10..2}`, `{01..12}`) and does not care what files exist; it runs before variables are expanded.
- `$(cmd)` is replaced by cmd's stdout; `$((expr))` by an integer result.
- Unquoted results are word split on space, tab and newline (`IFS`), then globbed.
- Double quotes allow only the `$` expansions; single quotes allow none.

topics.title: Your first scripts: shebang, running, comments, arguments
topics.examNote: Quiz 1 Q2E: *from inside a script, how can you print the number of command line arguments?* (`echo $#`). Every long question on Quiz 1 was a script (Q4 copy permissions, 4 marks; Q5 `trash.sh`, 10 marks) built on today's basics: the shebang, `$1`, `$2` and quoting. Those two also need variables (Day 4). On the paper exam you write scripts by hand, so practise typing them out from memory.

blocks.text:
A **Bash script** is a plain-text file that holds a list of commands. When you run the script, Bash reads the file and runs the commands one after another, exactly as if you had typed them at the prompt. So **anything you can type in the terminal can go in a script**: paths, globs, quoting, redirections, pipes and expansions all work inside scripts too.

The course naming conventions for script files:

- end with `.sh` (for example `hello.sh`)
- start with a lowercase letter
- use only letters, digits and `_`, with `_` between words (for example `make_backup.sh`)

### Your first script, step by step

**Step 1: open a new file in a text editor.** Use the editor from Day 1. Make a folder for your scripts, go into it, and open a new file named `hello.sh`:

blocks.code:
$ mkdir -p ~/scripts
$ cd ~/scripts
$ gnome-text-editor hello.sh
blocks.caption: Use gedit hello.sh on older Ubuntu, or nano hello.sh inside the terminal.

blocks.text: **Step 2: type the script.** Type these three lines exactly (the middle line is empty):

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash

echo 'Hello, world!'
blocks.caption: hello.sh

blocks.text:
The first line, `#!/bin/bash`, is called the **shebang** (or *hash-bang*, from the two characters `#` and `!`). It must be the **very first line**, with `#!` as the first two characters (no blank line or space before it). It tells the operating system which program should run the rest of the file: here `/bin/bash`, the Bash shell. On the exam, **start every script with `#!/bin/bash`**.

**Step 3: save.** Press **Ctrl + S** and close the editor (in nano: Ctrl + O, Enter, Ctrl + X). Back in the terminal, check what you saved:

blocks.code:
$ cat hello.sh
#!/bin/bash

echo 'Hello, world!'
$ ls -l hello.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 user1 user1 34 Sep 15 10:00 hello.sh
blocks.caption: A new file has no x (execute) permission yet.

blocks.text: **Step 4: make it executable.** A script file must be **readable and executable** for you to run it by name. If you try too early, the shell refuses:

blocks.code:
$ ./hello.sh
bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod u+x hello.sh
$ ls -l hello.sh
-rwxr--r-- 1 user1 user1 34 Sep 15 10:00 hello.sh
blocks.caption: chmod u+x (Day 2) adds execute permission for the owner, you. chmod +x hello.sh also works: it adds x for everyone.

blocks.text:
You only need to `chmod` a script **once**. Editing and saving it again later keeps its permissions.

**Step 5: run it from its folder.** Type `./` followed by the file name:

blocks.code:
$ ./hello.sh
Hello, world!

blocks.text:
`./hello.sh` means "the file `hello.sh` in the current directory `.`". You need the `./` because, for a bare command name like `ls`, the shell only searches the directories listed in your *path*, and the current directory is normally not one of them. `./hello.sh` is a relative pathname, so the shell does not search: it runs exactly that file. Any other pathname works too, for example `~/scripts/hello.sh` from any folder.

You can also run a script with `bash hello.sh`. That starts a new Bash and hands it the file as an argument, so it works **even without execute permission** (Bash only needs to *read* the file).

Do steps 1 to 5 now: create `~/scripts/hello.sh`, try `./hello.sh` before `chmod` and read the error, then `chmod u+x hello.sh` and run it again. Finally run `cd ~` and try `./hello.sh` from there: read that error too.

blocks.q: You saved `hello.sh` in the current directory. Give the two commands that make it executable for you and then run it.
blocks.a: `chmod u+x hello.sh` then `./hello.sh`. (Without execute permission you could still run it with `bash hello.sh`.)

blocks.text:
### When it doesn't run: reading the error message

| You see | What it means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied` | The file exists but has **no execute permission**. | `chmod u+x hello.sh` (or run `bash hello.sh`). |
| `bash: ./hello.sh: No such file or directory` | There is **no file with that name in the current directory**: you are in the wrong folder, or the name is misspelled. | Run `pwd` and `ls`; `cd` to the script's folder, or type its full pathname. |
| `hello.sh: command not found` | You left out the `./`, so the shell searched the path and did not look in the current directory. | Type `./hello.sh`. |
| `cannot execute: required file not found` (older Bash: `bad interpreter: No such file or directory`) | The **shebang line is wrong**, for example `#!/bin/bsh`: the program it names does not exist. | Fix the first line to read exactly `#!/bin/bash`. |

blocks.q: Why does typing just `hello.sh` usually give `command not found`, while `./hello.sh` works?
blocks.a: A bare name is searched for only in the directories on the path, and the current directory is normally not on it. `./hello.sh` is a pathname, so the shell does not search: it runs exactly that file.

blocks.q: Your script is `~/scripts/count.sh` and your terminal is in `~`. You type `./count.sh` and get `No such file or directory`. Give two ways to run it.
blocks.a: `cd ~/scripts` and then `./count.sh`, or type its pathname from where you are: `scripts/count.sh` (or `~/scripts/count.sh`). `./count.sh` looked for the file in `~`, where it is not.

blocks.text:
### Any command can go in a script

The notebook's `fortunecow.sh` is a one-line pipeline (`fortune | cowsay -f moose`). Its `makesh.sh` does something useful: it creates a skeleton script named `tmp.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

echo '#!/bin/bash' > tmp.sh
chmod u+x tmp.sh
```

Running it prints nothing (the Unix *rule of silence*: quiet on success), but `ls` afterwards shows the new, executable `tmp.sh`. The `'#!/bin/bash'` is in single quotes, so it is just text that `echo` writes into the file.

### Comments

`#` starts a **comment**: the shell ignores the `#` and everything after it to the end of the line. Use comments to say what the script does. They can be on their own line or after a command:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# makesh.sh: create a skeleton script named tmp.sh

echo '#!/bin/bash' > tmp.sh    # write the shebang into tmp.sh
chmod u+x tmp.sh
```

Two details:

- A **quoted or escaped** `#` is not a comment. `echo '# This is not a comment'` prints `# This is not a comment`.
- A comment always runs **to the end of the line**, so you cannot put one in the middle of a command. `ls #list_all_.txt_files .txt` is just `ls`.

(The shebang starts with `#` too: to Bash it is a comment, but the operating system reads it first.)

Every command sets an **exit status** (Day 1): `0` for success, `1` to `255` for failure, read with `$?`. A script sets one too: the status of the **last command it ran**. The notebook's `comment.sh` contains only comments, so it runs nothing and succeeds. (How a script chooses its own exit status comes on Day 5.)

blocks.code:
$ ./comment.sh
$ echo $?
0
blocks.caption: comment.sh contains only the shebang and comments.

blocks.q: What does the script line `ls *.txt # list text files` run?
blocks.a: `ls *.txt`. Everything from `#` onward is a comment, so it is ignored.

blocks.text:
### Command line arguments: positional parameters

Scripts take command line arguments like any other command (`./greet.sh Sam`). Bash stores them in **positional parameters** and a few **special parameters**, and you get their values with `$`, just like `$?`:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$0` | the pathname used to run the script, e.g. `./args.sh` |
| `$1`, `$2`, ... `$9` | the first, second, ... ninth argument |
| `${10}`, `${11}`, ... | the tenth argument and later: **braces required** |
| `$#` | the **number** of arguments (not counting `$0`) |
| `"$@"` | all the arguments, each kept as a separate word |

You cannot assign to these with `=`; the shell sets them when the script starts. Asking for an argument that was not given is **not an error**: `$3` just expands to the empty string.

Suppose `args.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# args.sh: show the arguments

echo "$# arguments: first=$1 second=$2"
echo "called as $0"
```

blocks.code:
$ ./args.sh "a b" c
2 arguments: first=a b second=c
called as ./args.sh
$ ./args.sh
0 arguments: first= second=
called as ./args.sh

blocks.text: Notice that `"a b"` is **one** argument: the quotes on the command line kept the space inside it (Day 2). The quotes themselves are not part of `$1`. The parameters are inside double quotes in the script, and double quotes still allow `$` expansions.

Create `args.sh` in `~/scripts` with the editor, `chmod u+x args.sh`, and run it as `./args.sh`, `./args.sh one two three` and `./args.sh "one two" three`. Predict `$#` each time before you press Enter.
`$10` is **not** the tenth argument. Bash reads it as `$1` followed by the character `0`. With arguments `a b c d e f g h i j`, `echo "$10 ${10}"` prints `a0 j`. Always write `${10}`, `${11}`, ...

blocks.q: A script is run as `./s.sh one "two three" four`. What are `$#`, `$2` and `$0`?
blocks.a: `$#` is `3`, `$2` is `two three`, and `$0` is `./s.sh`.

blocks.text:
Quiz 1 Q2E asked: *from inside a script, how can you print the number of command line arguments?* Answer: `echo $#`.

The notebook's `hellou.sh` greets whoever is named in the first argument. Braces are always allowed around a parameter name: `${1}` is the same as `$1`.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# hellou.sh

echo "Hello, ${1}!"
```

`./hellou.sh Sam` prints `Hello, Sam!`; with no argument it prints `Hello, !`.

### Arguments in a pipeline

Arguments make a pipeline reusable: the user chooses the file. This script prints the three smallest student numbers of any class list named by `$1`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# lowest3.sh: the three smallest student numbers in class list file $1

cut -f3 "$1" | sort | head -n3
```

Always write `"$1"` **with double quotes** where a file name goes. Unquoted, a name with a space such as `class list 2` would be word split into the three arguments `class`, `list` and `2` (yesterday's quoting lesson and today's word splitting).

blocks.caption: classlist is the 4-line file from the Streams lesson.

blocks.q: Write the one command line (after the shebang) of a script that prints the number of lines in the file named by its first argument, and nothing else.
blocks.a: `wc -l < "$1"` (with `<`, `wc` prints only the number). `wc -l "$1"` would also print the file name.

blocks.text:
### All the arguments: `"$@"` (and `$*`)

`"$@"` (**with** the double quotes) expands to all the arguments as separate words, exactly as given: `"$1" "$2" "$3" ...`. It is the safe way to pass every argument on to another command:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# countlines.sh: count the lines of every file named on the command line

wc -l "$@"
```

blocks.code:
$ ./countlines.sh classlist "my notes.txt"
 4 classlist
 2 my notes.txt
 6 total
blocks.caption: my notes.txt has 2 lines. Each argument reached wc as one word, space and all.

blocks.text: Without the quotes, `$@` is word split, so the argument `my notes.txt` becomes the two words `my` and `notes.txt`, and `wc` complains that neither exists. `"$*"` joins all the arguments into **one** string separated by spaces; you will rarely want that. You will use `"$@"` most with `for` loops on Day 6.

blocks.q: A script runs `ls -l "$@"`. It is called as `./l.sh "a b" c`. What arguments does `ls` receive?
blocks.a: Two: `a b` and `c`. With `ls -l $@` (unquoted) it would receive three: `a`, `b` and `c`.

blocks.text:
### Putting it together

The notebook improves `makesh.sh` so the user chooses the file name with `$1`. With the quoting the course requires:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# namedsh.sh: create an executable skeleton script named $1

echo '#!/bin/bash' > "$1"
chmod u+x "$1"
```

Running `./namedsh.sh myscript.sh` creates `myscript.sh` containing the shebang, with execute permission for the owner.

### Script tasks in the drills

From today the drills (`./drill.sh start 3`) include **script tasks**. Their header says where to save the file, for example `(script: write ~/cisc220_drills/scripts/day3/greet.sh)`.

1. Open that exact file in your editor: `gnome-text-editor ~/cisc220_drills/scripts/day3/greet.sh` (the folder was made by `./drill.sh start 3`).
2. Write the script, starting with `#!/bin/bash`, and save it.
3. Run `./drill.sh check 3`. You do **not** need `chmod` for this: the checker **copies** your script into a fresh sandbox folder (the one named in the task, usually `home/user1`, where files like `classlist` are), **makes it executable**, and runs test commands there such as `./greet.sh Sam`. It runs the reference solution the same way and compares standard output, standard error, the exit status and the files left behind.

To try your script by hand first, copy it into your practice sandbox and run it there:

```bash
cd ~/cisc220_drills/play/day3/home/user1
cp ~/cisc220_drills/scripts/day3/greet.sh .
chmod u+x greet.sh
./greet.sh Sam
```
Run `./drill.sh start 3` in the `drills` folder, read the first script task, write the script in `~/cisc220_drills/scripts/day3/`, and run `./drill.sh check 3`.

### Key points

- Write the script in an editor, first line `#!/bin/bash`, save; `chmod u+x f.sh` once; run it from its folder with `./f.sh` (or `bash f.sh`).
- `Permission denied` = no execute permission; `No such file or directory` = no such file in the current folder (or a wrong shebang).
- `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line, unless it is quoted.
- `$1`...`$9`, then `${10}`; `$#` is the number of arguments (`echo $#`); `$0` is how the script was called; `"$@"` is all arguments, separately.
- Quote arguments where file names go: `cut -f3 "$1"`. A script's exit status is that of its last command.

flashcards.front: File descriptor numbers of stdin, stdout, stderr?
flashcards.back: 0 = standard input, 1 = standard output, 2 = standard error.

flashcards.front: How do you end keyboard input to a command like `sort`?
flashcards.back: Press Ctrl-d (end of input).

flashcards.front: Command to overwrite `myfile` with the string OOPS (Quiz 1)
flashcards.back: `echo OOPS > myfile`
`>` creates or **overwrites** the file; `>>` creates or **appends** to it.

flashcards.front: Is the `1` in `1> file` required?
flashcards.back: No. `> file` means `1> file`. The `2` in `2> file` **is** required.

flashcards.front: Redirect only the error messages of `cmd` to `err.txt`
flashcards.back: `cmd 2> err.txt`

flashcards.front: Send stdout of `cmd` to out.txt and stderr to err.txt
flashcards.back: `cmd > out.txt 2> err.txt`

flashcards.front: Send both stdout and stderr of `cmd` to `all.txt`
flashcards.back: `cmd > all.txt 2>&1` (bash shorthand: `cmd &> all.txt`).

flashcards.front: What does `2>&1` mean?
flashcards.back: Make fd 2 (stderr) a copy of fd 1 (stdout): send errors to wherever stdout points **at that moment**.

flashcards.front: In what order does the shell process redirections?
flashcards.back: Left to right. So `> f 2>&1` sends both to f, but `2>&1 > f` leaves errors on the terminal.

flashcards.front: What is `/dev/null`?
flashcards.back: The null device: a file that discards everything written to it (and reports success).

flashcards.front: Run `cmd` but throw away its error messages
flashcards.back: `cmd 2> /dev/null`

flashcards.front: How does a script print an error message on stderr?
flashcards.back: `echo "message" >&2`: `>&2` (short for `1>&2`) sends echo's stdout to fd 2.

flashcards.front: Print only the number of lines in `classlist` (no file name)
flashcards.back: `wc -l < classlist`

flashcards.front: What does a pipe `|` connect?
flashcards.back: The **stdout** of the left command to the **stdin** of the right command. stderr is not piped.

flashcards.front: What does `tee file` do?
flashcards.back: Copies its stdin to stdout **and** to the file(s) named, so a pipeline can save an intermediate result and keep going.

flashcards.front: Why is `sort data > data` a bug?
flashcards.back: The shell truncates `data` before sort runs, so sort reads an empty file and data ends up empty.

flashcards.front: `sort -n` vs `sort`
flashcards.back: `-n` sorts numerically (9 before 10); plain sort compares as text (10, 100, 9).

flashcards.front: What does `uniq` remove? What does `uniq -d` print?
flashcards.back: `uniq` removes **adjacent** duplicate lines (sort first). `uniq -d` prints one copy of each duplicated line only.

flashcards.front: Default field delimiter of `cut`
flashcards.back: The TAB character. Use `-d` to choose another, e.g. `cut -d" " -f1` or `cut -d: -f1`.

flashcards.front: Pipeline: student numbers (field 3) of classlist, sorted, all saved to snum, print first three
flashcards.back: `cut -f3 classlist | sort | tee snum | head -n3`

flashcards.front: Count the distinct lines of words.txt
flashcards.back: `sort words.txt | uniq | wc -l`

flashcards.front: The seven expansions in order
flashcards.back: 1 brace, 2 tilde, 3 parameter, 4 command substitution, 5 arithmetic (4 and 5 same precedence, left to right), 6 word splitting, 7 filename expansion.
`a1 a2 b1 b2`

flashcards.front: Create directories week01 ... week12 in one command
flashcards.back: `mkdir week{01..12}` (leading zeros are kept).

flashcards.front: `n=3; echo {1..$n}` prints?
flashcards.back: `{1..3}`: brace expansion runs before parameter expansion, so `{1..$n}` is not a valid sequence.

flashcards.front: What does `~` expand to? `~bob`?
flashcards.back: Your home directory (`$HOME`). `~bob` is bob's home directory.

flashcards.front: What is command substitution?
flashcards.back: `$(command)`: runs the command in a subshell and replaces itself with the command's stdout (trailing newlines removed).

flashcards.front: Store the output of `date` in variable `now`
flashcards.back: `now=$(date)`

flashcards.front: What is arithmetic expansion? `echo $((7 / 2))`?
flashcards.back: `$(( expr ))` evaluates integer arithmetic and substitutes the result. Prints `3` (integer division).

flashcards.front: What is word splitting?
flashcards.back: Unquoted results of expansions are split into separate words at IFS characters (space, tab, newline by default); runs of separators count as one.

flashcards.front: Which expansions happen inside double quotes?
flashcards.back: Only parameter `$x`, command substitution `$( )` and arithmetic `$(( ))`. No brace, tilde, word splitting or filename expansion.

flashcards.front: Which expansions happen inside single quotes?
flashcards.back: None. Every character is literal.

flashcards.front: Why does the course always write `"$var"`?
flashcards.back: Double quotes stop word splitting and filename expansion, so the value is passed as one argument exactly as stored (spaces, `*` and all).

flashcards.front: How do you store a value in a variable and use it (just enough for today)?
flashcards.back: `name=value` with **no spaces** around `=`, then `$name` for the value. `n=3; echo $n` prints `3`.

flashcards.front: What must the first line of a Bash script be, and what is it called?
flashcards.back: `#!/bin/bash`, the **shebang** (hash-bang). It names the program that interprets the script.

flashcards.front: How do you make `go.sh` executable for yourself and run it from its directory?
flashcards.back: `chmod u+x go.sh` (once), then `./go.sh`

flashcards.front: How can you run `go.sh` without execute permission?
flashcards.back: `bash go.sh` (Bash only needs to read the file).

flashcards.front: Why `./go.sh` and not just `go.sh`?
flashcards.back: Bare names are looked up only in the directories on the path, which normally does not include the current directory. `./go.sh` is a pathname to the file.

flashcards.front: What character starts a comment, and where does the comment end?
flashcards.back: `#`; it runs to the end of the line. A quoted or escaped `#` is not a comment.

flashcards.front: The steps to create and run your first script `hello.sh`
flashcards.back: 1. `gnome-text-editor hello.sh` (or gedit / nano) 2. first line `#!/bin/bash`, then the commands 3. save (Ctrl + S) 4. `chmod u+x hello.sh` 5. `./hello.sh` from the same folder.

flashcards.front: `./go.sh` prints `Permission denied`. What is wrong?
flashcards.back: go.sh has no execute permission. Fix: `chmod u+x go.sh` (or run it with `bash go.sh`).

flashcards.front: `./go.sh` prints `No such file or directory`. What is wrong?
flashcards.back: There is no `go.sh` in the current directory: wrong folder or misspelled name. Check with `pwd` and `ls`, then `cd` to its folder or type its full pathname. (If the shebang names a program that doesn't exist, you get a similar "not found" error.)
The pathname used to run the script, e.g. `./trash.sh`.
The first, second, ..., ninth command line argument (empty if not given).

flashcards.front: How do you get the tenth argument? What does `$10` mean?
flashcards.back: `${10}`. `$10` is `$1` followed by the character `0`.
The number of command line arguments (not counting `$0`). Quiz 1: print it with `echo $#`.
All the command line arguments, each as a separate word, exactly as given: `"$1" "$2" ...`
`"$*"` joins all arguments into one string separated by spaces; `"$@"` keeps them as separate words.
The exit status of the most recently completed command (0 = success, 1-255 = failure).

flashcards.front: What is a script's exit status when it simply runs to the end?
flashcards.back: The exit status of the last command it ran (check it with `echo $?` right after).

flashcards.front: Is using an argument that was not given (e.g. `$3` with 2 arguments) an error?
flashcards.back: No. It expands to the empty string.

flashcards.front: Why write `cut -f3 "$1"` rather than `cut -f3 $1` in a script?
flashcards.back: The double quotes stop word splitting, so a file name with spaces (e.g. `class list 2`) stays one argument.

flashcards.front: Drill script tasks: where do you save the script, and do you need `chmod`?
flashcards.back: In `~/cisc220_drills/scripts/day3/NAME.sh`. No `chmod`: the checker copies it into the task's sandbox folder, makes it executable and runs the tests there.

quiz.q: What single command overwrites the contents of a file named `report` with the string `EMPTY`? Use a redirection.

quiz.q: Starting in an empty directory, what does this print?

cat f

options: Nothing; both lines are in out.txt
Both the line `a` and the error message

quiz.q: You just saved `hello.sh` (permissions `rw-r--r--`) in the current directory. Which command runs it **without** changing its permissions?
quiz.explain: `bash hello.sh` only needs read permission. `./hello.sh` fails with `Permission denied` until you `chmod u+x hello.sh`. Plain `hello.sh` is searched for on the path (not the current directory). `run` is not a command.

quiz.q: You wrote `count.sh` and saved it. Running `./count.sh` prints `bash: ./count.sh: Permission denied`. What fixes it?
quiz.explain: Permission denied means the file has no execute permission. A file you just created is already readable by you, so `u+r` changes nothing. Without `./` the shell searches the path and reports `command not found`. The shebang is not the problem.

quiz.q: `hello.sh` is in `~/scripts` and is executable. Your terminal is in `~`. You type `./hello.sh` and get `No such file or directory`. Why?
options: The script has no execute permission
There is no `hello.sh` in the current directory `~`
Scripts can only be run with `bash hello.sh`
quiz.explain: `./hello.sh` means *the file hello.sh in the current directory*. Run `cd ~/scripts` first, or type `scripts/hello.sh`. A missing execute permission gives `Permission denied` instead.

quiz.q:
`args.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
echo "$#: $1 | $2"
```

What does `./args.sh "a b" c` print?
quiz.explain: The quotes make `a b` a single argument, so there are 2 arguments, `$1` is `a b`, and `$2` is `c`.

quiz.q:
`count.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
echo $#
```

What does this print?
quiz.explain: `$#` counts the arguments: `a`, `b c` (one argument, thanks to the quotes), the empty string `''` (still an argument) and `d`.

quiz.q:
`ten.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
echo "$10 ${10}"
```

What does this print?
quiz.code: ./ten.sh a b c d e f g h i j
quiz.explain: `$10` is `$1` (`a`) followed by the character `0`. Only `${10}` gives the tenth argument, `j`.

quiz.q: From inside a script, how do you print the number of command line arguments? (Quiz 1)
quiz.explain: Accept `echo "$#"` or `echo ${#}`.

quiz.q:
`classlist` contains these 4 lines, fields separated by single TABs:

```
Cade	Barry	3100025
Day	Holly	2999999
Friese	Andy	3001111
Yu	Sue	1990000
```

`first.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
cut -f2 "$1" | sort | head -n "$2"
```

What does this print?
quiz.explain: `$1` is `classlist` and `$2` is `2`. Field 2 is the first names; sorted they are Andy, Barry, Holly, Sue; `head -n 2` keeps two.

quiz.q:
`show.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# show.sh
echo "$0 was given $# arguments"   # count them
echo "$@"
```

What does this print?
quiz.answer:
./show.sh was given 2 arguments
one two  three
quiz.explain: `$0` is the pathname used to run the script. The extra spaces between arguments on the command line just separate words, so there are 2 arguments. `"$@"` passes them to echo separately; echo joins them with one space, and the two spaces inside `two  three` are kept because they are part of that argument. The comment prints nothing.

write.prompt:
The file `scores` has one line per student: name, section and score, separated by TAB characters. For example:

```
Ahmed	002	88
Blake	001	9
Chen	001	100
```

Write a **single pipeline** that extracts the scores, sorts them from **highest to lowest** (numerically), saves **all** of the sorted scores in a file named `ranked`, and prints only the **top five** scores.
write.solution: cut -f3 scores | sort -n -r | tee ranked | head -n5
write.explain:
Translate each phrase, in order:

1. *extracts the scores*: the score is field 3 and the delimiter is TAB, which is `cut`'s default: `cut -f3 scores`.
2. *highest to lowest, numerically*: `sort -n -r`. Without `-n`, 9 would sort above 88 because text comparison sees `9` > `8`.
3. *saves all of the sorted scores*: `tee ranked`. It must come **after** sort (the file must be sorted) and **before** head (the file must contain every score).
4. *prints only the top five*: `head -n5`.

`sort -nr` and `head -n 5` are equally correct.

rubric.item: `tee ranked` placed between sort and head, then `head -n5`

pitfalls: Using `> ranked` in the middle of a pipeline: it sends the output to the file and nothing reaches head.

write.prompt:
Write a script `firstn.sh` that is run as `./firstn.sh FILE N`. It prints one line `FILE has L lines` (where L is the number of lines in FILE), and then the first N lines of FILE in **sorted** order. File names may contain spaces.

Example: `./firstn.sh classlist 2` prints

```
classlist has 4 lines
Cade	Barry	3100025
Day	Holly	2999999
```
write.solution:
#!/bin/bash

# firstn.sh: show how long FILE is, then its first N lines in sorted order

echo "$1 has $(wc -l < "$1") lines"
sort "$1" | head -n "$2"
write.explain:
1. `#!/bin/bash` first, always.
2. `$1` is FILE and `$2` is N: the shell sets them from the command line.
3. The message is one `echo` with a command substitution inside double quotes. `wc -l < "$1"` prints only the number; `wc -l "$1"` would add the file name. The double quotes inside `$( )` are fine: they belong to the inner command.
4. *First N lines in sorted order* means sort first, then cut it down: `sort "$1" | head -n "$2"`. Doing `head` first would sort only the first N lines of the file.
5. Every `$1` and `$2` is quoted, so a file name like `class list 2` stays one argument.

rubric.item: `echo` with `$1` and a command substitution giving only the line count (`wc -l < "$1"`)

pitfalls: `head -n "$2" "$1" | sort` sorts only the first N lines of the file, not the whole file.
`$(wc -l "$1")` puts the file name into the message twice.
Writing `$(wc -l < $1)`: unquoted, a file name with a space breaks.

write.prompt: A program `./build.sh` prints normal messages to standard output and error messages to standard error. Fill in the blanks so that each command does what its comment says.
write.starter:
# (a) normal output to out.txt, errors to err.txt
./build.sh ____ out.txt ____ err.txt

# (b) both normal output and errors into log.txt
./build.sh > log.txt ____

# (c) normal output on the terminal, errors thrown away
./build.sh ____
write.solution:
# (a) normal output to out.txt, errors to err.txt
./build.sh > out.txt 2> err.txt

# (b) both normal output and errors into log.txt
./build.sh > log.txt 2>&1

# (c) normal output on the terminal, errors thrown away
./build.sh 2> /dev/null
write.explain: (a) `>` (or `1>`) redirects fd 1 and `2>` redirects fd 2. (b) After stdout points at log.txt, `2>&1` makes stderr a copy of it; the order matters. (c) `/dev/null` discards whatever is written to it.
pitfalls: Writing `> /dev/null` in (c), which throws away the normal output instead.

write.prompt:
Fill in the blanks using **expansions**.

(a) Create the directories `A1`, `A2`, ..., `A6` with one mkdir command.

(b) Print `There are N files here` where N is the number of names that `ls` prints in the current directory.

(c) Print the number of minutes in a week (let the shell compute it).
write.starter:
mkdir A____
echo "There are ____ files here"
echo ____
write.explain: (a) A sequence brace expansion with the preamble `A`. (b) Command substitution runs the pipeline and inserts its output; it still works inside double quotes. (c) Arithmetic expansion computes 10080.
pitfalls: Writing `$(7 * 24 * 60)`: single parentheses are command substitution and try to run a command named 7.
Single-quoting the sentence in (b) stops the substitution.

write.prompt:
Fill in the blanks of `info.sh` so that each line prints what its comment says. For example, `./info.sh red "light blue"` should print

```
script: ./info.sh
count: 2
first: red
```

and then a long listing (`ls -ld`) of the files named by **all** the arguments, each argument kept whole.
write.starter:
#!/bin/bash

# info.sh: describe how the script was called

echo "script: ____"    # the pathname used to run the script
echo "count: ____"     # the number of arguments
echo "first: ____"     # the first argument
ls -ld ____            # every argument, each as one word
write.solution:
#!/bin/bash

# info.sh: describe how the script was called

echo "script: $0"    # the pathname used to run the script
echo "count: $#"     # the number of arguments
echo "first: $1"     # the first argument
ls -ld "$@"            # every argument, each as one word
write.explain: `$0` is the pathname used to run the script, `$#` the number of arguments (Quiz 1 Q2E: `echo $#`), `$1` the first argument. `"$@"` (with the quotes) passes every argument as a separate word, so `light blue` reaches `ls` as one name.
pitfalls: Writing `$@` without quotes: `light blue` is split into `light` and `blue`.
Confusing `$0` (the script's pathname) with `$1` (the first argument).

write.prompt:
Write a script `snumsave.sh` that takes two command line arguments: `$1` is the name of a classlist file (last name TAB first name TAB student number) and `$2` is the name of an output file. The script

1. writes the student numbers, sorted in ascending order, into the file named by `$2` (overwriting it), and
2. prints the message `saved N student numbers` where N is the number of lines in that output file.
write.explain: The first line is a pipeline whose final stdout is redirected into the output file. The second line uses command substitution; `wc -l < file` prints only the number (no file name). Nested double quotes inside `$( )` are fine.

rubric.item: `> "$2"` at the end of the pipeline
Command substitution with `wc -l` that yields only the number (`< "$2"` or `cut -f3 "$1" | wc -l`)

pitfalls: `wc -l "$2"` inside the message prints `saved 4 out.txt student numbers`.
`sort > "$2" "$1"` style mix-ups: keep the redirection at the end of the pipeline.

write.prompt:
Write a script `mkweeks.sh` that is run as `./mkweeks.sh COURSE`. Assume the directory COURSE does not exist yet. The script

1. creates the directory COURSE containing the twelve directories `week01`, `week02`, ..., `week12`, using **one** `mkdir` command, and
2. prints the line `COURSE: N folders` where N is counted by the script itself with `ls` and `wc` (it should be 12).

The name COURSE may contain spaces.

Example: `./mkweeks.sh CISC220` creates `CISC220/week01` ... `CISC220/week12` and prints `CISC220: 12 folders`.
write.explain: `-p` creates COURSE as well as the week directories inside it. The brace expansion is outside the quotes (braces do not expand inside quotes), while `"$1"` is quoted; written side by side they make one word per week, such as `CISC220/week01`. `ls "$1" | wc -l` counts the names inside COURSE. `mkdir "$1" "$1"/week{01..12}` is equally correct.

rubric.item: One `mkdir` that also creates COURSE (`-p`, or `"$1"` listed first)
`week{01..12}` brace expansion (leading zeros) after `"$1"/`, with `$1` quoted

pitfalls: `"$1/week{01..12}"`: inside quotes the braces are not expanded, so one directory named `week{01..12}` is made.
Forgetting `-p`: mkdir cannot create `CISC220/week01` before `CISC220` exists.
